articles.title: Venezuela‘s interim president Delcy Rodríguez promises election after Maduro ousted
articles.summary: The opposition in Venezuela has slammed her for not setting even a tentative date for elections.
articles.body:
Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has announced that elections will be held as part of a transition to "full democracy", but did not specify a date.

Rodríguez was sworn in just days after her predecessor in office, Nicolás Maduro, was seized by US forces and taken to New York to face drug-trafficking charges.

She has enjoyed the backing of the Trump administration despite her previously close ties to Maduro.

The opposition in Venezuela has slammed her for not setting even a tentative date for elections.

Critics of her government have long denounced the 2024 election, after which Maduro was declared president and she vice-president, as fraudulent and say they have vote tallies to back up their claim .

Speaking at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Rodríguez insisted that "there will be elections in Venezuela" and that the Venezuelan people would determine "the right moment" when to hold them.

The interim president, who was a close ally of Maduro and served as his vice-president until his ouster by the US, did not mention the jailed former leader once.

Less than nine months after the US raid on the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in which the presidential couple was seized and about 100 people killed, she instead thanked US President Donald Trump "for his willingness to take the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation".

She also said that her government and the Trump administration were "working seriously to resolve existing differences through dialogue", adding that the two nations were paving "the way for energy relations, the promotion of security, the common fight against transnational crime and economic cooperation for the benefit of both peoples and our continent".

Unlike Rodríguez, President Trump did make ample references to Maduro during his speech to the assembly, calling him an "outlaw dictator, a real criminal".

Trump also celebrated the signing of what he said was "the largest oil deal in history covering 65bn barrels of oil" which the US has struck with Rodríguez's interim government.

"To the victor belong the spoils," he stated, adding that "if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interest of the United States".

While he did not mention elections in his speech at the UN, Trump told the LA Times earlier this month that he did not think Venezuela was ready yet.

The two leaders also briefly met Tuesday on the sidelines.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who attended the meeting, said that the two presidents had discussed elections. However, he appeared to urge Venezuelan opposition politicians to be patient.

Rubio insisted that first, there would have to be a "political transition process" to rebuild the institutions necessary to have free and fair elections.

"What we don't want to see (…) would be that someone is elected, and they inherit a complete catastrophe, economic and social," he said.

Rubio also pointed to negotiations under way between Venezuela's interim government and some members of the opposition as a sign of progress.

Critics of the negotiations have, however, pointed out that Venezuela's most prominent opposition leader, María Corina Machado, is not part of the talks.

Machado, who left Venezuela in December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo, has not been able to return to the country since.

One of her advisers said that she had made three attempts to travel to her home country this week but that all three had been thwarted.

Machado remains barred from standing for office - a ban imposed under the Maduro government - and Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello has in the past said that should she return, the authorities would have "a surprise" in store for her.

articles.title: Texas triple murderer uses last words before execution to send message to death row inmates
articles.summary: Ker'Sean Ramey received lethal injection at Huntsville prison, one week after accomplice LeJames Norman was executed for the same triple killing.
articles.body: A man convicted of murdering three people in their apartment while searching for drugs to steal was executed in Texas on Wednesday evening, a week after his accomplice was put to death for the same killings. Ker'Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection at the state penitentiary in Huntsville and was pronounced dead at 6:34 p.m. CDT, The Associated Press reported. In the execution chamber, a prison chaplain rested his hand on Ramey's shoulder before leading him in a brief prayer. The warden then asked Ramey if he had any last words, the AP reported. Ramey praised God and thanked his friends, family and fellow death row inmates, whom he called his brothers. ARIZONA EXECUTES MAN WHO KILLED VICTIM BY DOUSING HIM IN GASOLINE AND SETTING HIM ON FIRE IN 2002 ATTACK "To the brothers on Texas death row that grew up with me, that poured into me and showed what it means to be a man, because I came in young, and didn’t understand what manhood was... to you brothers... I greatly appreciate you," Ramey said moments before the injection was prepared. As the pentobarbital took effect, Ramey took a deep breath, sputtered and began snoring. After 10 loud snores and two that were barely audible, he went still. He was pronounced dead 14 minutes after the injection was first administered. Ramey became the sixth inmate executed in Texas this year, with the state set to carry out three more lethal injections over the next two months. In January 2007, Ramey was convicted and sentenced to death for the August 2005 shootings of Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, at a home they shared in Edna, a small rural city about 100 miles southwest of Houston. 74-YEAR-OLD BECOMES FLORIDA'S OLDEST INMATE EXECUTED AFTER 1982 KILLING OF TEEN LeJames Norman, Ramey's accomplice, lived across the street from the house and the two came to believe there was cocaine there, according to court records. On Aug. 24, 2005, the men walked over to the home while wearing masks and knocked on the door. After Lopez answered the door, they forced their way inside, records show. After finding no drugs, the two men fatally shot Lopez, then killed Peacock and Roberts when they arrived at the home. Before fleeing for good, Ramey returned and shot the victims again to ensure they were dead, according to court documents. Norman was executed on Sept. 16 at the Huntsville prison, where all executions are carried out in Texas. MANHATTAN PROSTITUTE PLEADS GUILTY TO KILLING 3 MEN WITH FENTANYL-LACED DRUGS IN ROBBERY SCHEME Hours before Ramey was put to death, the Supreme Court rejected his final appeal. Ramey's attorneys argued jurors never heard mitigating evidence about his upbringing, including that he endured physical abuse as a child and grew up in poverty. State prosecutors urged the Supreme Court to reject the appeal, calling it "meritless" and arguing the record showed Ramey had exhibited an escalating pattern of criminal behavior. Norman was arrested about five months after the killings while attempting to re-enter the United States from Mexico, where he had fled. During Ramey's January 2007 trial, Norman testified that both men took part in the shootings, while Ramey's attorneys argued Norman was solely responsible. Norman pleaded guilty to capital murder and was sentenced to death in December 2008. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Rare Captain America and Batman comics were stored for 75-80 years; recently discovered collection heads to auction
articles.summary: A recently discovered collection of Golden Age comics, stored for roughly 75 to 80 years, is heading to auction.
articles.body: A recently discovered collection of Golden Age comics, stored for roughly 75 to 80 years, is heading to auction. According to Heritage Auctions, the original-owner Merrimack Valley Collection includes a 9.4 Captain America Comics No. 3, a 9.0 Captain America Comics No. 1 and the first nine issues of Batman. The books are among the highlights of Heritage's Sept. 24-26 Comic Books Signature Auction, with the first live floor session beginning at noon CT on September 24.Inside the recently discovered Merrimack Valley Collection of Golden Age comic booksThe Merrimack Valley Collection surfaced as an original-owner group of Golden Age comics that Heritage says had been stored for the last 75 or 80 years in a brown cardboard box. Heritage Auctions Vice President Aaron White described it as a "really, really exciting collection" and said the books were in terrific condition, with striking colours. The collection dates primarily to the early Golden Age of comics, and its original-owner provenance is part of what distinguishes the group. Heritage is offering the collection as part of its Sept. 24-26 Comic Books Signature Auction, which features more than 700 comic books spanning the 1930s to the present.Why these Captain America comics stand outAmong the collection's most notable books is a 9.4 copy of Captain America Comics No. 3, which Heritage describes as the second-finest known copy. The 1941 issue contains a text story by Stan Lee, marking what Heritage identifies as his first work for Timely Comics. Only seven of the 135 copies carry a grade of 9.0 or higher, according to Heritage's listing, and only one is graded higher than this 9.4 copy.The collection also includes a 9.0 Captain America Comics No. 1. Heritage says there are only two copies at the 9.0 grade, with six copies graded higher. The issue, published in 1941, is one of the key early Captain America comics and is currently ranked No. 7 on Overstreet's list of the Top 100 Golden Age Comics, according to Heritage.The collection includes Batman's first nine issuesThe Merrimack Valley Collection also contains the first nine issues of Batman, giving the collection an unusually substantial run of the character's earliest solo comic books. Heritage says eight of those nine issues received grades of 6.5 or higher. Among them are 9.0 copies of Batman Nos. 5, 7 and 9, all early-1940s issues. The Batman books form another major part of the collection's Golden Age offering alongside the two high-grade Captain America issues.When the Merrimack Valley Collection goes to auctionHeritage's Sept. 24-26 Comic Books Signature Auction is taking place this week, with the first Signature Floor Session covering lots 91001 through 91235. Heritage's current auction page lists the live session for 12:00 p.m. Central Time on Thursday, September 24, while proxy bidding ends at 11:50 a.m. CT. The auction continues through September 26 with additional sessions.The comic-book auction overlaps with Heritage's separate Sept. 25-27 Comic Art Signature Auction, which features original artwork rather than the printed comics in the Merrimack Valley Collection. Among its highlights is the opening splash page from Iron Man No. 1 by Gene Colan and Johnny Craig, consigned by Marvel Studios founding chairman David Maisel. Other featured pieces include Jerry Robinson's Detective Comics No. 68 cover and Jack Kirby's Fantastic Four No. 56 cover.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'No anti-incumbency against BJP?' Party counters Rahul Gandhi with Tamil Nadu, Bengal poll history
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's claim that anti-incumbency has “disappeared” for the BJP because of its alleged collusion with the Election
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's claim that anti-incumbency has “disappeared” for the BJP because of its alleged collusion with the Election Commission drew a sharp response from the ruling party. BJP national spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi cited the Congress's electoral record in states including Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha to hit back at leader of opposition in Lok Sabha.Rahul Gandhi, speaking at a press conference in New Delhi on Thursday amid the ongoing row over the Election Commission and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, questioned how anti-incumbency could seemingly affect successive governments but not the BJP.Responding to Rahul's remarks, BJP MP Sudhanshu Trivedi questioned his understanding of Indian electoral history and argued that the stronger long-term anti-incumbency trend was against the Congress."From a political point of view, his wisdom is zero, his knowledge is zero," Trivedi said, launching a personal attack on Rahul.Trivedi then pointed to states where the Congress has not returned to power for decades."Yes, anti-incumbency is indeed very strong and consistent against Congress," he said.On Tamil Nadu, Trivedi said the Congress had not returned to power since 1967, arguing that the BJP was not even a significant political force in the state at the time. In West Bengal, he said, the Congress had not returned to government since 1977.The Election Commission's statistical reports list assembly elections across the states and provide the historical electoral data on which such comparisons can be made.The BJP spokesperson also cited Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha, saying there had been no Congress government in Bihar after 1990, no Congress government in Uttar Pradesh after 1989 and no Congress government in Odisha since 1999."Ever since transparent elections have taken place, CCTV cameras have come in, and independent media has arrived, they've started finding it difficult to come to power," Trivedi said.What Rahul Gandhi saidEarlier in the day, Rahul held a press conference in which he cited former PM Indira Gandhi as an example, saying she was at the height of her popularity after the 1971 Bangladesh war but faced "massive anti-incumbency" within a year or two."The same thing happens to leader after leader, to Congress leaders and to regional parties. But, for some reason, it does not happen to PM Modi, Amit Shah and the BJP," Rahul Gandhi said.He also pointed to electoral changes in Haryana, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh, arguing that these states had historically seen voters shift between parties."Haryana swings from one party to another for 50 years, but suddenly anti-incumbency disappears. Maharashtra swings; suddenly that disappears. Uttar Pradesh swings, from the Samajwadi Party to the Bahujan Samaj Party, that also disappears," he said.Rahul said the question had been a "fundamental" one for the Congress until the party arrived at what he described as the answer: "vote chori".His remarks came as he stepped up his attack on the Election Commission over the SIR exercise. He accused chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of undermining the electoral process, demanded his resignation and alleged that the destruction of votes would ultimately undermine the Constitution and institutions."From vote chori comes kanoon chori, and from that comes sanstha chori," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Oracle is taking legal steps to protect itself from accumulating expenses on a massive artificial intelligence (AI) data center in southern New Mexico, marking a sharp escalation for an infrastructure project mired in public opposition and regulatory hurdles. Citing individuals familiar with the matter, a report by Bloomberg says that the enterprise technology giant has sent a formal notice citing force majeure to the project’s developer, a unit of alternative asset manager Blue Owl Capital. Following this development, Oracle’s shares fell 4%, losing millions of dollars from its market cap.The report notes that rather than walking away entirely as the anchor tenant, Oracle is seeking to defer contractual payments if the facility, internally named Project Jupiter, encounters further delays and misses its planned 2028 operational target.What is Force Majeure and understanding Oracle’s moveCompanies generally invoke force majeure to suspend or excuse contractual duties when uncontrollable events prevent performance. In this dispute, Oracle is asserting its contractual standing ahead of potential construction bottlenecks. However, it remains uncertain whether the maneuver will legally relieve Oracle of its earlier financial obligations.Addressing the situation publicly, an Oracle spokesperson affirmed the facility's target delivery, saying, “Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule. We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward.”The Stargate anchor and debtThe southern New Mexico facility was planned as a cornerstone of the broader Stargate AI infrastructure push. US President Donald Trump originally unveiled the venture alongside top executives from Oracle, OpenAI, and SoftBank Group, framing it during the early days of his second term as a historic investment unseen in modern tech history.Nearly two years later, the campus reportedly faces steep challenges. One of them is the massive energy scale. The hub was engineered to draw 2.45 gigawatts, which is equivalent to the steady electricity demand of roughly 1.8 million homes. The second is financing pressure as a syndicate of approximately 20 commercial banks backed the campus with an $18 billion construction loan, representing one of the largest debt packages financing the generative AI boom.Thirdly, even if deployed purely as a legal safeguard, Oracle's notice risks unnerving institutional debt holders. The debt backing the project is already trading at distressed levels below 90 cents on the dollar.The disclosure also highlights contractual vulnerabilities in hyperscale leases, where tech firms commonly reserve termination rights if developers miss committed handover dates. An earlier example occurred when Alphabet's Google contracted with Elon Musk's SpaceX for computing power through mid-2029 while retaining rights to exit if capacity failed to materialize on schedule.You use AI every day. articles.title: Activists found guilty of stealing King's lambs from Sandringham
articles.summary: They believed the King "would have consented to their rescue" due to being an "environmentalist".
articles.body:
Three animal rights activists have been found guilty of stealing three lambs from the King's Sandringham Estate.

Throughout a three-day trial, Rosa Sharkey, 26, Sarah Foy, 26, and Rose Patterson, 37, insisted they rescued the animals in 2023.

The members of campaign group Animal Rising also said they believed the King "would have consented to their rescue" due to being an "environmentalist".

But the jury of five men and seven women at Norwich Crown Court unanimously found all three guilty of theft. They were each sentenced to a 12-month community order of 150 hours of unpaid work, and they must each pay £250 towards prosecution costs.

Sentencing them, judge Anthony Bate said their actions highlighted "sensitive and important matters of public interest".

He added that the defendants were all "intelligent and capable women who can make a valuable contribution to society".

After the hearing, Patterson, director of Animal Rising, said: "We are of course disappointed by the verdict today, but it doesn't change how I feel about rescuing Sammy, Sunny and Sooty."

The theft took place on 23 May 2023, when the trio spent hours in a field at Appleton Farm in Sandringham, to allow the sheep to become acquainted to them.

The court heard they then took three lambs and put them into a van after they came close, and they were driven off to an unknown animal sanctuary.

The following day, the women travelled to Windsor Castle, where they attempted to alert authorities to what they called a "rescue" of the lambs.

They later handed themselves in to Windsor Police Station and were charged with theft.

Earlier in the hearing on Thursday, defence barrister Sarah-Jane Ewart, representing Sharkey, insisted the trio had acted "honestly" throughout.

She highlighted their attempt to alert the authorities at Windsor as an example.

In the trial, all three defendants detailed how their personal experiences had led them to become involved in animal rights activism, due to concerns about welfare and the environmental impact of agriculture.

The lambs have never been recovered by the authorities but remained alive and well at an unknown sanctuary, the court heard.

After the verdict, Patterson said the trio "rescued them because we believed they deserved the chance of a long life", adding: "I don't regret for a moment giving them that chance."

Sharkey added: "This isn't the verdict we hoped for, but the most important thing to me is that those three lambs were saved and are now living safely and happily."

articles.title: Developer fined £1m after man killed by falling window
articles.summary: Mick Ferris was crushed when the 130kg window fell from The Corniche building  in Vauxhall.
articles.body:
A property developer has been fined £1m after a window fell from a luxury riverside penthouse in south London and killed a coach driver.

Mick Ferris, 53, was crushed when the pane of glass weighing 130kg (20 stone) fell 26 storeys from The Corniche in Vauxhall on 2 October 2018.

His wife Rachel Ferris told the sentencing hearing at Inner London Crown Court that her husband's death "could have been prevented", after it emerged that a window fell from the same development in August 2017, but the design was not substantially changed as a result.

Mitigating for the developer St James Group Ltd, Prashant Popat KC said his client was "deeply remorseful and regretful".

The father-of-two was hit by the falling glass as he returned to his coach on central London's Albert Embankment that morning.

Specialist façade contractor Lindner Prater was also fined £300,000, after it and St James were found guilty of ignoring "foreseeable risks".

Luxury architecture firm Foster + Partners and engineering consultants Wintech Ltd were cleared of the same charge.

Judge Boyle said St James should have been more robust in "ensuring the critical safety component" of the window was "present and engaged".

He added that Lindner Prater "should have done more to complete and document the risk assessment process".

In addition to the fine, Judge Boyle ordered St James and Lindner Prater to pay costs of £125,000 each.

Ferris said her husband's death was "so sudden" and "out of the blue".

In a statement read out in court, she said: "If somebody had done something differently – anything – it would have changed our lives. We wouldn't be in this position.

"I know it wasn't just one person, but one person could have changed this.

"What those companies did killed my husband.

"The thought this could have happened to anybody is always with me. It could have been a child."

She also told the court that 400 people attended her husband's funeral, and said "he is missed by so many it was unbelievable".

At the time of the incident, television host and fellow West Ham fan James Corden paid tribute to Mick Ferris on Twitter , saying: "He was a huge West Ham fan and has passed away in the most sudden of circumstances."

He added: "Tell your loved ones you love them today."

HSE principal inspector James Goldfinch said: "The fact lessons had not been learnt from a near miss the year before makes what happened on that day all the more galling.

"For a window to fall once was quite extraordinary, for it to fall again was simply criminal."

articles.title: Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit against Des Moines Register over 2024 race
articles.summary: Trump had argued the Iowa polling company sought to damage his campaign by publishing an inaccurate poll.
articles.body:
An Iowa judge has dismissed President Donald Trump's lawsuit against The Des Moines Register and its former pollster over a poll that showed the president trailing former Vice-President Kamala Harris in the 2024 race.

The judge ruled that the poll was protected by the US Constitution, and dismissed the president's argument that pollster J Ann Selzer had engaged in "brazen election interference" and that the inaccurate prediction constituted fraud.

Trump had filed the lawsuit suit after he won the election in the state of Iowa by 14 points.

In a statement to US media, a spokesperson said the president was "committed to holding responsible those who traffic in deception and fake news".

Trump sought to "stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability", Judge Scott Beattie wrote in a 64-page ruling.

Judge Beattie added that allowing a "legally faulty claim like this" to go forward "carries a cost that an ordinary case does not, because defending it can discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs".

The president - who had accused the polling company of intentionally publishing an inaccurate poll - was joined by two Republicans, Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and former Iowa state Senator Brad Zaun, in his lawsuit.

"This scam was designed to damage President Trump's dominant campaign in the final days of the race," his spokesperson told US media. The BBC has contacted Trump's legal team for comment.

Selzer's polls have successfully predicted several election outcomes, including former President Barack Obama's sizeable win in the 2008 Iowa caucuses and the 2014 Senate election in Iowa.

But her polls have proven wrong on other occasions, including when she inaccurately predicted John Kerry to beat George W Bush in Iowa in the 2004 presidential election.

In a statement to US media after the ruling, Selzer said polling was a social science, not "clairvoyance".

"What we can guarantee is that we will follow the data wherever it leads, even when the results are uncomfortable or unexpected," she said. "I am grateful that Judge Beattie's ruling recognises these principles and reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference."

articles.title: 5th grade teacher, student die during field trip to nature reserve
articles.summary: Investigators are looking to determine what happened.
articles.body:
A fifth grade teacher and her student died during a field trip to an Iowa nature reserve this week, investigators and school officials said.

Hannah Jorgensen, 24, a fifth-grade teacher at Borlaug Elementary School in Coralville, and Ahmed Osman, 10, died while on the trip at the MacBride Nature Recreation Area on Tuesday, the Iowa City Community School District said in a statement.

The Johnson County Sheriff's Office received a call around noon of two persons in the water near the Coralville Reservoir spillway at the nature reserve, which is roughly eight and a half miles north of Iowa City.

The bodies of Jorgensen and Ahmed were eventually found in the reservoir, investigators said. The circumstances behind their deaths during the trip are still under investigation, according to the Johnson County Sheriff's Office.

"Hannah and Ahmed were deeply valued members of our school district community, and their loss is being felt throughout Borlaug and across our district," the Iowa City Community School District said in a statement Wednesday. "Our hearts are with their families and loved ones, as well as Hannah's colleagues and students, Ahmed's classmates and friends, and everyone who knew and cared for them."

Jorgensen's body was first discovered Tuesday and Osman's the next day, investigators said.

School officials said that counselors will be on hand to help with the school community.

"This is an extraordinarily painful time for the Borlaug community and our entire school district. We will continue to come together, care for one another, and keep Hannah, Ahmed, and their families at the center of our hearts in the difficult days ahead," the district said in a statement.

Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds also offered her condolences and support to the school community as the investigation into the incident continues.

"This unimaginable loss touches the entire Borlaug Elementary community and Iowa City School District. Please know that Iowans across our state are standing with you in the difficult days ahead," she said in the statement posted on Facebook.

articles.title: Man jailed for bottle throwing at Eastney migrant protest
articles.summary: Del Somerville, 42, pleaded guilty to violent disorder following an overnight protest at Eastney.
articles.body:
A father-of-two has become the first man jailed following an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth after admitting throwing a plastic bottle and swearing at police.

Del Somerville, 42, was given a two-year sentence after previously pleading guilty to violent disorder at the city's crown court following the overnight protest near Eastney Marina on 6 September.

Hundreds of protesters gathered after a boat carrying about 120 migrants was brought ashore near Eastney Beach.

He pleaded not guilty to a separate charge of assaulting a police officer, relating to an incident on 11 September, and will face trial at Portsmouth Magistrates Court at a later date.

Judge Daniel Sawyer told Somerville that his sentence would act as a deterrent to others following subsequent protests in the area.

Describing him as a "thug", he told the defendant: "Police officers dedicate their lives to the protection of the public regardless of their own views, the very least they can expect is that those who engage in protests treat them with respect and the courts punish those who assault them."

The court heard Sommerville, from Portsmouth, was among a large group of demonstrators protesting at the arrival of the migrants.

They were brought ashore by the RNLI after being picked up in the Channel. A number of volunteer lifeboat crew members were subject to online abuse following the incident.

Prosecutor Edward Warren said Somerville was part of an "initially peaceful and lawful" gathering of a number of people on Ferry Road.

At shortly before 23:30 BST, he was with a large group of men as they were held up by the police line.

The court was told he was identified in police body-worn video as throwing a small bottle and swearing at police.

When later interviewed by police, he said he had found the bottle on the ground and was going to throw it into a nearby bush, but was angry and so threw it up into the air.

Defence barrister Helen Easterbrook said Somerville had been "caught up" in the disturbances.

She said he had been attempting to be a "calming influence" on the crowd but had thrown the bottle "in frustration".

Four other men are awaiting sentence having also been charged with violent disorder following the protest in Eastney.

articles.title: An Alabama man fought a power company over a 74-mile transmission line planned across his 416-acre retirement property; after crews moved within 500 yards, a judge temporarily blocked them from entering
articles.summary: A landowner in Shelby County, Alabama, has won a temporary court order stopping utility crews from clearing land on his 416-acre retirement property.
articles.body: A landowner in Shelby County, Alabama, has won a temporary court order stopping utility crews from clearing land on his 416-acre retirement property. The order has paused construction work on part of a major regional power project. Circuit Judge Jonathan A. Spann issued a preliminary injunction blocking Alabama Power from entering Fenn Church's property. The utility plans to build a 125-foot-wide right of way for a new 74-mile power line. The court order requires Church to post a $10,000 bond while his larger legal challenge moves through the courts. The ruling stopped power company contractors who had already started clearing trees and earth about 500 yards from Church's property line in Calera. According to local television station WVTM 13, Judge Spann said Church could face immediate and irreparable harm if crews continued working before the dispute received a final ruling. The court found that Church was likely to succeed in claims that Alabama Power did not follow required procedures before starting condemnation proceedings, especially rules about the timing and content of its final offer letters.Standing firm against eminent domainChurch bought the 416-acre farm in Calera four years ago with plans to build a retirement home. The property contains old-growth trees, wetlands, and Buxahatchee Creek. After the two sides failed to reach an agreement, Church rejected three separate purchase offers and Alabama Power began condemnation proceedings under state eminent domain laws. Court records show that the planned route would divide Church's land into six separate parcels. It would also give the utility access to his main private driveway for heavy equipment. Reporting by 1819 News showed that Church proposed other routes. One option would move the line 200 yards and use existing, cleared utility easements nearby. The utility rejected the proposed changes. Church publicly called the fight a "David and Goliath situation" as he worked to protect his property rights, local wildlife, and privacy. His legal battle later received wider national attention after country music singer John Rich promoted his cause on social media.Flaws identified in utility proceduresDuring a two-day hearing in Shelby County, lawyers presented evidence about how Alabama Power handled its condemnation notices. According to the written court order published by the Trussville Tribune, Judge Spann noted that Church received the formal final offer letters only after Alabama Power had already filed its condemnation lawsuit. The court found that this timing denied the landowner certain rights provided by state law. The judge also said Church was likely to succeed in arguments that the selected route and access roads were arbitrary and capricious. The court said utility planners did not properly consider future land use, possible development, or small changes to the route that could have avoided major damage to the property. Alabama Power engineers testified during the hearing that the 74-mile transmission project, running from Autaugaville to East Pelham, is intended to reduce strain on the electrical grid and improve regional power reliability. The company said contractors needed access to Church's land by October to meet a planned May 2027 completion date. However, Judge Spann wrote that the larger project remains on schedule. He said Alabama Power can continue work on other available sections of the route while Church's lawsuit is being decided.Protecting private property rightsAlabama Power says its policy is to reach voluntary agreements with property owners whenever possible. The company uses court-supervised condemnation only when negotiations fail. In a public statement about the lawsuit, Alabama Power said: "We understand that property is personal. We have demonstrated our commitment to treating property owners fairly and respectfully throughout this process." Despite those assurances, Church raised concerns in court filings about Alabama Power's ability to lease easement access to third-party telecommunications companies. Such an arrangement could allow outside traffic to use his private driveway. After the judge issued the preliminary injunction, Church described the order as an important victory for private property owners facing utility land seizures. The preliminary injunction will remain in place while the court sets a date for hearing Church's main lawsuit, which challenges the validity of the condemnation. articles.title: Greek PM Mitsotakis urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles
articles.summary: Andy Burnham said in 2023 the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".
articles.body:
The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece.

Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".

The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.

Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.

The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles.

"Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday .

"Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."

His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.

Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does."

"Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.

Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.

This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".

Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".

British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century.

They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens.

After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin's actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament.

The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal.

The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum.

Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a "more co-operative arrangement" after "quite a bitter disagreement" with the Greeks for more than 200 years.

Mitsotakis's latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again.

Last month, Greece's health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces.

The British Museum's position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common.

Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority.

He said only a probe could establish the amount involved and determine where the money went.Badal also announced that an SAD government would fill three lakh vacant government posts after assuming office, with recruitment restricted to Punjabis.He said the law permitting recruitment of outsiders would be repealed. articles.title: Xi Jinping tests Donald Trump with 'Thucydides Trap'
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: Implicitly suggesting that China is catching up with the United States if it hasn't already, Chinese President Xi
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: Implicitly suggesting that China is catching up with the United States if it hasn't already, Chinese President Xi Jinping told Americans on Thursday that the two countries can avoid the historic conflict that often accompanies the rise of a new power, declaring that “the Thucydides Trap CAN be overcome.”The phrase “Thucydides Trap” was coined by Harvard political scientist Graham Allison, drawing on the Athenian historian Thucydides' account of the Peloponnesian War.Thucydides identified the rise of Athens and the fear it generated in Sparta as the underlying force that made war increasingly difficult to avoid.Allison subsequently applied the historical pattern to modern great-power rivalry, examining 16 cases in which a rising power challenged an established one; in his analysis, 12 ended in war.Speaking at the White House welcome ceremony with President Trump sitting beside him, Xi said the US and China should pursue cooperation rather than confrontation and argued that China's rise need not come at America's expense.He called for the two countries to be “partners, not rivals,” arguing that China's “great rejuvenation” and Trump's ambition to “make America great again” could proceed together.China and the US should pursue a relationship in which competition is moderate, differences are manageable, and peace is predictable.It was hardly the language of a country preparing to surrender the geopolitical stage, nor was it quite the language of an adversary. It was Xi's preferred formulation of the relationship: two great powers, different systems, competing interests — but neither destined to destroy the other.But it implicitly placed the burden of avoiding the trap on the established power, which may resist treating the rise of the challenger as an existential threat.Trump, for his part, responded with warmth that belied his past demonisation of China. In vapid remarks, he described Xi as a “great leader” and emphasised the personal relationship between the two men, saying the US and China had a “great relationship.”It was a strikingly different tone from the confrontational rhetoric – not just from Trump but from many American leaders – that has characterised the US approach to China in recent years.While Beijing portrays China's rise as an opportunity for cooperation rather than a challenge requiring containment, critics in Washington counter that China's military expansion, pressure around Taiwan and growing strategic influence demonstrate that the United States cannot simply assume benign intentions.Many of them are blasting Trump for being a “Deferential President”, as the Atlantic magazine put it in a headline, while sneering, “Not long ago, President Trump could claim that he ran the world. Now he’s waiting at the bottom of a set of airline steps for the Chinese president.”But a more sobering perspective came from secretary of state Marco Rubio, who earlier in the day asserted that it would be irresponsible not to engage Beijing at the highest level despite differences.“The relationship between the United States and China will define the 21st century,” Rubio said, echoing words that the US till recently had used for its ties with India, which is probably watching the scenario with consternation.You use AI every day.
